claims.text: Local chemical short-range order in multi-component concentrated alloys creates nanoscale spatial fluctuations in generalized planar or stacking-fault energy.
Fault-energy fluctuations produce local hard atomic motifs that impede or pin moving dislocations.
Local chemical order and fault-energy fluctuations force dislocations to adopt irregular, wavy glide configurations.
The rugged fault-energy landscape raises activation barriers and lattice friction for dislocation motion.
The increased barrier to dislocation motion elevates alloy strength.
SRO-induced dislocation barriers cause more effective dislocation storage.
SRO-induced fault-energy fluctuations increase the work-hardening rate.
Increased work hardening delays deformation localization or necking.
SRO-induced fault-energy fluctuations enhance ductility.
A well-annealed CrCoNi-type concentrated alloy can retain significant local chemical order.
Alloy processing conditions can vary the amount of local chemical order.
Severe plastic deformation reduces local chemical order toward a random solid solution.
Low-temperature annealing promotes stable SRO, whereas high-temperature annealing suppresses or randomizes it.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates the proposed alloys under the stated ambient and optional cryogenic test conditions.
Suppressing SRO makes the generalized fault-energy landscape more spatially uniform.
Relative to an identically composed low-SRO baseline, a high-SRO sample will have a higher yield strength.
Relative to the low-SRO baseline, a high-SRO sample will exhibit a higher work-hardening rate.
TEM will reveal more wavy or pinned dislocation segments in the high-SRO material, spatially aligned with SRO-rich regions.
The proposed mechanism should apply to concentrated alloys having chemistry or size differences sufficient to produce measurable SRO.
The magnitude of SRO and its associated fault-energy landscape is sensitive to processing history.

contradictions.description: Severe plastic deformation is proposed as a way to randomize SRO while the comparison is also required to have identical grain size and microstructural background aside from SRO. Severe plastic deformation ordinarily changes defect density, dislocation structure, texture, and often grain size, so the stated route conflicts with the claimed isolation of SRO unless additional controls or matched post-processing are specified.
